Q: Is a value stored in registers/memory an address or the contents? A:

What does mov eax, 23h do? Does it store the value 23h to eax register or the address 23h (in eax)?

This instruction loads EAX with the value 23h (in hexadecimal notation), which is 35 in decimal notation. What the value represents is up to the user to decide, so it could in effect be an address...

value Word 230

What will mov ax, value do?

This will load AX with the (unsigned) value 230.
If you would like to load AX with the address of value then you would write mov ax, offset value, or alternatively (and one byte longer) lea ax, value.

Lastly what if we write mov ax, [value]?

This will still load AX with the value held at the address value. The square brackets in MASM don't make this any different than mov ax, value.
Confusing brackets in MASM32 has more on this.

Q: How can I connect to MgGraphs and Exchange Online in the same PowerShell session? A:

Very possible that the cause is an assembly conflict between Graph and Exchange Online modules and either one implements an assembly load context... what you can try is updating both modules to their latest version and hope after that they both end up using the same version of the conflicting assembly, if that didn't work there is a common workaround using an outside process (Start-Job makes it pretty easy) to do the work with one of the conflicting modules:

Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'Application.ReadWrite.All', 'Directory.ReadWrite.All'
# Ask Admin the email of the user being deactivated
$User = Read-Host 'What account is being deactivated?'

# Disable account
$Disable = @{ AccountEnabled = 'false' }
Update-MgUser -UserId $User -BodyParameter $Disable

# No need to disconnect from Graph, connect to exchange in a different process:
Start-Job {
    Import-Module ExchangeOnlineManagement
    Connect-ExchangeOnline

    # Hide from GAL and convert to shared mailbox
    Set-Mailbox -Identity $using:User -Type Shared -HiddenFromAddressListsEnabled $true

    # Set Auto-reply message
    $setMailboxAutoReplyConfigurationSplat = @{
        Identity        = $using:User
        AutoReplyState  = 'Enabled'
        InternalMessage = 'Thank you for your message.'
        ExternalMessage = 'Thank you for your message.'
    }

    Set-MailboxAutoReplyConfiguration @setMailboxAutoReplyConfigurationSplat
} | Receive-Job -Wait -AutoRemoveJob

# Remove Licenses
$License = Get-MgUserLicenseDetail -UserId $User
$LicenseData = @{
    addLicenses    = @()
    removeLicenses = @($License)
}
Set-MgUserLicense -UserId $User -BodyParameter $LicenseData

Q: GDB: Pretty-Print class containing STL container A:

On this page of the documentation you can see the function gdb.default_visualizer. It asks GDB to find pretty printer for the given value using its standard mechanisms, so you don't need to mess with the internals of libstdc++.

With this code:

class FooContainerPrinter(object):
    ...
    def children(self):
        pp = gdb.default_visualizer(self.val['content'])
        return pp.children()

I get the following printout for print c:

$1 = My Foo Container = {[0] = X: -13, [1] = X: -5, [2] = X: 1, [3] = X: 2, [4] = X: 17}

Q: Excel Hyperlink function to open a specific page A:

Here's how I got a particular PDF and page to launch from an Excel cell:

(Had Claude write this up for me, so excuse the odd tone ;) )

Instead of hyperlinks, I use a couple of macros that let you double-click a cell to launch — via the Worksheet_BeforeDoubleClick handler. A regular hyperlink can open a file, but it can't tell Acrobat which page to jump to, so the hyperlink route is a dead end for this. The double-click approach gets around that.

The flow: when a double-click is caught, the Worksheet_BeforeDoubleClick handler kicks in and fires off the macro that gets you to the right PDF and page.

How I set up my sheet

Three columns:

  • one column with the file path
  • another column with the page number
  • a third column that's the launcher cell

Instead of a hyperlink, we just monitor for double-clicks in that launcher column. That launcher cell is basically a button — it doesn't matter what's in it; the macro only cares that you double-clicked in that column, and it uses the row you clicked to know which file path and page to read.

(In my sheet: file path in column S, page number in column T, and I double-click in column T. Swap in your own columns — the code finds them by number.)

The simple version

Private Sub Worksheet_BeforeDoubleClick(ByVal Target As Range, Cancel As Boolean)
    If Target.Column = 20 Then
        Cancel = True
        JumpToPdf
    End If
End Sub

Public Sub JumpToPdf()
    Dim pdfPath As String, pdfPage As Long
    pdfPath = ActiveSheet.Cells(ActiveCell.Row, 19).Value   ' file path (column S)
    pdfPage = ActiveSheet.Cells(ActiveCell.Row, 20).Value   ' page number (column T)
    Shell """C:\Program Files\Adobe\Acrobat DC\Acrobat\Acrobat.exe""" & _
          " /A ""page=" & pdfPage & """ """ & pdfPath & """", vbNormalFocus
End Sub
  • Worksheet_BeforeDoubleClick is a standard Excel event handler — Excel fires it automatically whenever you double-click a cell on this sheet, and hands it the clicked cell as Target.
  • If Target.Column = 20 checks the click was in the launcher column (20 = column T); if not, nothing happens.
  • Cancel = True stops Excel's normal double-click behavior (dropping into edit mode on the cell).
  • JumpToPdf reads the file path and page from the row you clicked (ActiveCell.Row), then shells out to Acrobat with the /A "page=N" switch, which opens that file at that page.

The sturdier version

The version above leans on ActiveCell to figure out which row was clicked. It works — the double-click selects the cell — but it's cleaner to pass the sheet and the clicked row straight from the event, so the worker never has to guess:

Private Sub Worksheet_BeforeDoubleClick(ByVal Target As Range, Cancel As Boolean)
    If Target.Column = 20 Then
        Cancel = True
        JumpToPdf Me, Target.Row
    End If
End Sub

Public Sub JumpToPdf(ByVal ws As Worksheet, ByVal r As Long)
    Dim pdfPath As String, pdfPage As Long
    pdfPath = ws.Cells(r, 19).Value   ' file path (column S)
    pdfPage = ws.Cells(r, 20).Value   ' page number (column T)
    Shell """C:\Program Files\Adobe\Acrobat DC\Acrobat\Acrobat.exe""" & _
          " /A ""page=" & pdfPage & """ """ & pdfPath & """", vbNormalFocus
End Sub
  • The handler now passes Me (the sheet) and Target.Row (the clicked row) into JumpToPdf.
  • JumpToPdf uses exactly what it was handed — no reliance on whatever happens to be selected.

Notes

  • Placement: Worksheet_BeforeDoubleClick must go in the sheet's own code module (double-click the sheet in the VBA Project pane), because it's a worksheet event. JumpToPdf goes in a regular Module.
  • Acrobat path: adjust the path to Acrobat.exe if yours differs. The /A "page=N" command-line switch works with Acrobat and also Adobe Reader.
  • Columns: change the 19 / 20 and the Target.Column = 20 check to match wherever your file-path, page, and launcher columns actually are.
